newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuanians deliver snub as poll turnout falls.
newsitem.headline: Lithuanians deliver snub as poll turnout falls.

text.p: Lithuanian voters on Sunday seemed to have delivered a snub to their politicians as turnout figures for the second election since the country regained its independence from the former Soviet Union slumped.

Independence hero Vytautas Landsbergis had hoped to make this election his comeback after being rejected at the ballot box four years ago in favour of the ex-Communists of the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP).
But Lithuanians seemed instead to have expressed disillusionment and cynicism abut the political establishment six years after quitting the former Soviet Union.
By 1900 hrs local (1600 GMT), two hours before polls closed, voter attendance was at just over 50 percent, compared with 70 percent at the 1992 election.
Total turnout in 1992 was 75 percent but the vote then came at a time of economic collapse and political confusion.
Lithuanians on Sunday were voting in the first round of elections, with a second run-off set for November 10.
The first round decides 70 of the 141 parliament seats under a proportional system and the second round the rest under a majority vote.
First results are expected at around 0200 local (2300 GMT).
Landsbergis spearheaded Lithuania's independence drive from the former Soviet Union but was dumped by voters as the economy collapsed and his party was riven by in-fighting.
Landsbergis was quick on Sunday to blame voter apathy on four years of rule by the ex-Communists.
"It indicates disappointment with democratic institutions...It is the bad result of a bad job," he told Lithuanian television.
The LDLP came to power on a platform of easing the pain of reform but instead followed a path of austerity prescribed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
They have also been accused of corruption and croneyism.
They were badly hurt at the end of last year after a former prime minister withdrew his savings from a bank days before it was shut at the start of a banking crisis.
Political commentators had predicted Lithuanians may choose to register a protest against established political parties for failing to provide any new ideas.
Many people say they have failed to notice big changes in their lives and have little confidence in government.
Foreign Minister Povilas Gylys, a leading LDLP figure, blamed the low turnout on general pessimism.
"Many of our former supporters are disillusioned because they do not see improvements in their social security," he said.
A low turnout was thought by parties to favour Landsbergis's Homeland Union, whose supporters tend to vote early and are most disciplined.
Opinion polls had indicated the Homeland Union would become the largest party in parliament but would not get enough votes to form a government on their own.
They have already said they will work with the Christian Democrats, who stress traditional values in this Roman Catholic country.
But it was not clear which parties likely to make it into parliament the Homeland Union could work with.
Cheslovas Jurshenas, LDLP speaker of parliament, stressed the difference between the 1992 and 1996 elections.
"This time all was quiet," he said on television. "This is all about the charm and the lessons of democracy," he added.
